lines.text: Spring came to Greyhollow three weeks early. Nobody in the village could remember that happening before.
The debt was paid. The glasshouses were full. Tobin's lamps were selling in three cities. For the first time in its history, Greyhollow had money.
So, naturally, everyone wanted some.
My lord! Vaskan merchants want rimeglass. Southern lords want rimeglass. A bishop has written asking for rimeglass candles. I don't know what that means, but he's offering a fortune.
Tobin can make two lamps a week. That's the limit.
Then hire more blacksmiths!
There are no more blacksmiths. There are thirty-seven people, and one of them is nine.
That was the real problem. Greyhollow was too small. We needed people.
As it turned out, people needed us too.
They started arriving in the second week of spring. Families from burned villages in the east. Runaway serfs. A miller whose lord had taken his mill. All of them had heard the same rumour.
They say the lord of Greyhollow feeds everyone. They say nobody here goes cold.
My lord, there are forty more at the gate. Do we turn them away?
Do we have food?
With the glasshouses? For a hundred more, easily.
Then open the gate.
By midspring, Greyhollow had a hundred and twelve people. We built twenty new houses. Tobin took four apprentices. Wren taught archery to anyone who would hold a bow.
And every one of them, within a month, was healthier than they'd ever been in their lives. Good food, I thought. Fresh air. Honest work.
Your lord collects people the way a fire collects moths, Steward.
He collects strays. Always has. Look at me.
I'm meant to send my report to the capital by the end of spring.
And will you?
I haven't decided.
And then, one morning, a rider came from the south, wearing my father's colours.
A letter for Lord Lucan, from Lord Varr.
I knew my father's handwriting. Short. Cold. Exactly four lines.
House Corrow has crossed the River Senn with two thousand men. Maric marches to meet them. Every vassal of House Varr is summoned. Bring your levy.
My levy. My father was calling up Greyhollow's soldiers. A hundred and twelve farmers, a third of them children.
He meant it as a formality. A joke, probably. Nobody expected the zero to bring anyone at all.
I looked out of the window. At Wren, drilling thirty archers in the yard. At Tobin's forge, glowing blue. At Oswin, teaching sword drills to men who had been serfs a month ago.
Bram. How many of ours can fight?
All of them, my lord. All of them.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter ten, coming soon.
